subject: Critical Thinking
title: Correlation vs. Causation: Together Doesn't Mean Because
description: A quick, practical guide to Correlation vs. Causation: Together Doesn't Mean Because.

hook.text: Ice cream sales and drowning deaths both rise in summer. Does ice cream cause drowning? No. Heat causes both.

buildup.text: Correlation: two things happen together. Causation: one thing causes the other. They look identical but aren't.

discovery.text: A hidden third variable (confound) often explains both. Or the causation runs backwards. Or it's pure coincidence.

twist.text: A famous spurious correlation: US spending on science correlates 99.79% with suicides by hanging. Obviously meaningless.

climax.text: To prove causation, you need controlled experiments, temporal precedence, and elimination of alternative explanations.

punchline.text: Together doesn't mean because. Always ask: what else could explain this?

quiz.question: Why doesn't correlation prove causation?
options: A third variable, reverse causation, or coincidence could explain the relationship

details.summary: Correlation means two things happen together; causation means one causes the other. Ice cream sales and drowning both rise in summer, but ice cream does not cause drowning. Confusing the two is one of the most common reasoning errors.
details.whyItMatters: Most published health scares, business insights, and social media claims confuse correlation with causation, leading to false beliefs and bad decisions.
takeaways: Co-occurrence does not prove a causal relationship
A third variable often explains both correlated phenomena
Controlled experiments are needed to establish causation

faq.question: What is the most common reason people confuse correlation with causation?
faq.answer: The brain is a pattern-detection machine that instinctively assigns causal explanations to patterns. When two things co-occur repeatedly, the brain assumes one causes the other because that was a useful survival heuristic in ancestral environments.

faq.question: What techniques can help establish whether a correlation is actually causal?
faq.answer: Randomized controlled experiments are the gold standard. When experiments are impossible, look for dose-response relationships, temporal precedence (cause before effect), and elimination of plausible confounders.
